lessons.title: Recognise and continue patterns
lessons.summary: Count the fixed and repeated parts of diagrams, follow a term-to-term rule and compare two patterns.
lessons.objective: Count the fixed and repeated parts of diagrams, follow a term-to-term rule and compare two patterns.
lessons.before: For Core and Extended. Number positions from 1 and distinguish the position from the term value.
lessons.ideas:
A drawing can change in one place and stay the same somewhere else. Count those two parts separately.

A term-to-term rule tells you what to do to one value to get the next. It needs a starting value before you can use it.

Some patterns have their own rule for the gaps. For other patterns, add the two terms immediately before the gap.

Place the position numbers above the terms before you compare. A relationship between two patterns usually refers to matching positions.
lessons.method:
How do I count the part that grows?

In the lights diagram each stage adds one panel containing three lights. The two end lights stay in every stage. The first three totals are 5, 8 and 11.

What operation takes me to the next term?

For a constant-step pattern, subtract the earlier term from the later one. Keep the sign. For alternating rules, identify which of the two actions comes next.

What if the gaps change or I need two terms?

If the gaps increase by the same amount, extend the row of gaps first. If the rule says to add the two previous terms, use their values directly.

How can I compare two patterns?

If pattern B has twice as many pieces as A plus three more, find A at the required stage first. Double its count and add three.
mistakes: The end lights appear once at every stage. They do not belong inside the part that repeats.
Subtracting in reverse order changes the sign. An increasing sequence has a positive difference and a decreasing one has a negative difference.
A new gap is a change, not the next term. Add it to the last term to reach the next one.
The change from one position to the next and the change from one pattern to another are different comparisons.

examples.title: Count the fixed and repeated parts of a pattern
examples.question: A row of signs has 9 end lights altogether. At stage \(n\) it also has 3 lights in each of \(n\) repeated panels. The first three totals are \(12,\;15,\;18\). How many lights are there at stage 14?
examples.solution:
The panels give \(3n\) lights at stage \(n\). The end lights do not change.

Use \(3n+9\). For stage 14, the total is \(51\).

examples.title: Continue a constant-step sequence
examples.question: These terms have a constant difference. Write the next term in \(-19,\;-15,\;-11,\;-7\).
examples.solution:
Subtract one term from the term that follows it. Each change is \(4\).

Add that signed change to \(-7\) to get \(-3\).

examples.title: Continue a pattern of changing gaps
examples.question: The sequence starts \(17,\;24,\;32,\;41\). Its positive gaps form a linear sequence. Find the next term.
examples.solution:
The first three gaps are \(7,\;8,\;9\). They go up by 1 each time, so the next gap is 10.

Add it to the last term, \(41\), to get \(51\).

examples.title: Use a relationship between two patterns
examples.question: Two strips grow in stages. Strip A has \(26,\;32,\;38\) tiles at stages 1 to 3 and grows by 6 tiles each stage. At the same stage, strip B has twice as many tiles as A, plus 9. Find the number of tiles in strip B at stage 4.
examples.solution:
Strip A has \(44\) tiles at stage 4.

Double that stage's value and add 9. Strip B has \(97\) tiles.

lessons.title: Find and use a linear nth term
lessons.summary: Find the common difference and constant, then evaluate a later term or decide whether a value occurs.
lessons.objective: Find the common difference and constant, then evaluate a later term or decide whether a value occurs.
lessons.before: For Core and Extended. Number positions from 1 and distinguish the position from the term value.
lessons.ideas:
A linear sequence has a constant difference \(d\). Its position-to-term formula has the form \(dn+c\).

The subscript in \(T_n\) labels the position. It tells you which number to substitute.

Set the formula equal to the stated value and solve for the position. A valid position is a positive whole number.
lessons.method:
How can I write one rule for every position?

Find the common difference first. At position 1, \(dn\) already gives \(d\). Use the gap between that value and the actual first term to find \(c\).

How do I find a term far down the sequence?

Use the nth-term rule directly. For example, if \(T_n=37-4n\), substitute \(n=9\) to give \(T_9=1\).

How can I tell whether a value occurs?

If solving gives a fractional or non-positive position, explain what this means for the sequence. Substitute a possible position back into the rule to check it.
mistakes: The adjustment \(c\) need not equal the first term. The expression must give the first term when \(n=1\).
A decreasing sequence can go through zero into negative terms. Its position numbers are still positive integers.
Rounding a fractional position changes the term value. State that the target does not occur.

examples.title: Find the rule for any position
examples.question: Find the \(n\)-th term of the linear sequence \(9,\;7,\;5,\;3\). Give an expression in \(n\).
examples.solution:
The difference is \(-2\). Start with \(-2n\).

When \(n=1\), the formula must give \(9\). The adjustment is \(11\), so the rule is \(-2n+11\).

examples.title: Use a formula to jump to a later position
examples.question: Sequence \(A\) has \(A_n=6n+24\). Find \(A_{16}\).
examples.solution:
The subscript tells you which position to use. Substitute \(n=16\).

The result is \(120\).

examples.title: Find the position of a given term
examples.question: A sequence has \(T_n=10n-14\). At which position does the term \(96\) occur?
examples.solution:
Set the term formula equal to \(96\). Solve \(10n-14=96\).

After removing the constant, divide by the common difference to get \(n=11\).

lessons.title: Find simple quadratic and cubic rules
lessons.summary: Match simple quadratic and cubic patterns to squares and cubes and check the resulting formulas.
lessons.objective: Match simple quadratic and cubic patterns to squares and cubes and check the resulting formulas.
lessons.before: For Core and Extended. Number positions from 1 and distinguish the position from the term value.
lessons.ideas:
Write the square numbers \(1,\;4,\;9,\;16,\;25\) underneath the given values at positions 1 to 5.

The first cubes are \(1,\;8,\;27,\;64,\;125\). Compare them with the given terms at the same positions.

A shifted power sequence can start at a later square or cube. The first position still has \(n=1\).
lessons.method:
How can square numbers help me find the rule?

For a rule of the form \(an^2+b\), the second difference equals \(2a\). Divide by 2 to find the scale. Subtract the scaled squares to find the same leftover in each position.

How can cube numbers help me find the rule?

For \(an^3+b\), the third difference equals \(6a\). Subtract the scaled cubes. If the same value remains each time, that value is the constant adjustment.

What if the starting power is not the first square or cube?

If the first two values are \(4^2\) and \(5^2\), the base at position 1 is 4 and the base at position 2 is 5. The rule is \((n+3)^2\).
mistakes: The first difference of a quadratic is not constant. Compare the differences between those first differences.
A large jump is not enough to show a cubic rule. Compare with the cube numbers or check the third differences.
Add the position shift before squaring or cubing. Adding outside the power changes every term in a different way.

examples.title: Compare a simple quadratic sequence with squares
examples.question: The sequence \(22,\;31,\;46,\;67\) is obtained by scaling the squares and then adding a fixed number. Find its \(n\)-th term.
examples.solution:
The squares at the same positions are \(1,\;4,\;9,\;16\). The second difference is \(6\), so the scale is \(3\).

Subtract the scaled squares from the given values. The leftover is always \(19\). The rule is \(3n^2+19\).

examples.title: Compare a simple cubic sequence with cubes
examples.question: The sequence \(19,\;47,\;123,\;271\) is obtained by scaling the cubes and then adding a fixed number. Find its \(n\)-th term.
examples.solution:
The cubes at the same positions are \(1,\;8,\;27,\;64\). The third difference is \(24\), so the scale is \(4\).

Subtract the scaled cubes from the given values. The leftover is always \(15\). The rule is \(4n^3+15\).

examples.title: Use a shifted power sequence
examples.question: The first terms are \(125,\;216,\;343,\;512\). The rule uses consecutive cube numbers. Find the term at position 14.
examples.solution:
The first term is \(5^3\). The base is always the position plus 4.

At position 14 use \((14+4)^3=5832\).

lessons.title: Build richer quadratic and cubic rules
lessons.summary: Extended: use second and third differences, then find the lower-power terms from the residual sequence.
lessons.objective: Extended: use second and third differences, then find the lower-power terms from the residual sequence.
lessons.before: For Extended. Check that you can find and use a linear rule and recognise square and cube numbers.
lessons.ideas:
For \(an^2+bn+c\), the constant second difference is \(2a\). It gives only the leading coefficient.

For \(an^3+bn^2+cn+d\), the constant third difference equals \(6a\).

The completed formula has a contribution from each lower power that was found. Substitute the same position into every part.
lessons.method:
How do I find more than the quadratic part?

Remove \(an^2\) from the given terms at the same positions. Find the remaining linear rule from its difference and first value. Add the two expressions together.

How do I handle a cubic rule with several parts?

Subtract \(an^3\) from the original values. Use the second differences of the remaining row to find the quadratic part. Repeat for the linear part and constant.

How do I check the complete rule?

Check the first term and another term from the list. If your model misses at a later position, trace which part of the residual row was not accounted for.
mistakes: A correct leading term can still give a wrong first term. Work with the full row of residual values.
Use the residual row to find the next coefficient. The original second differences of a cubic are not constant.
Finding a rule that works at only one position does not identify the whole sequence.

examples.title: Separate the leading power in a quadratic sequence
examples.question: The sequence \(8,\;11,\;18,\;29\) follows a quadratic rule. Find its \(n\)-th term.
examples.solution:
The first differences are \(3,\;7,\;11\). The second differences are \(4,\;4\). Divide the constant difference by 2 to get \(2\).

Subtract \(2n^2\) at the same positions. The remaining values are \(6,\;3,\;0,\;-3\).

The remaining linear rule has difference \(-3\). Fit its constant using position 1.

Add back the leading power. The full rule is \(2n^2-3n+9\).

examples.title: Separate the leading power in a cubic sequence
examples.question: The sequence \(10,\;33,\;96,\;217,\;414\) follows a cubic rule. Find its \(n\)-th term.
examples.solution:
The first differences are \(23,\;63,\;121,\;197\). The third differences are \(18,\;18\). Divide the constant difference by 6 to get \(3\).

Subtract \(3n^3\) at the same positions. The remaining values are \(7,\;9,\;15,\;25,\;39\).

The residual second difference is \(4\). It gives coefficient \(2\) of \(n^2\). Remove that part and fit the remaining linear rule.

Add back the leading power. The full rule is \(3n^3+2n^2-4n+9\).

examples.title: Use every part of a higher-degree rule
examples.question: A sequence has \(T_n=4n^2+2n+9\). Find \(T_{17}\).
examples.solution:
Use \(n=17\) in every term, including any lower-power terms.

Find each power and then combine the products and constant. The value is \(1199\).

lessons.title: Find and use exponential rules
lessons.summary: Extended: identify a constant multiplier, write the exponential nth term and interpret the exponent as a number of steps.
lessons.objective: Extended: identify a constant multiplier, write the exponential nth term and interpret the exponent as a number of steps.
lessons.before: For Extended. Check that you can find and use a linear rule and recognise square and cube numbers.
lessons.ideas:
An exponential sequence multiplies each term by the same factor. Divide one term by the previous one to find the common ratio.

There are no steps before the first term. With first term \(a\) and ratio \(r\), write \(T_n=ar^{n-1}\).

Divide the target term by the starting term. Find how many repeated factors the result contains.

A positive multiplier below 1 makes positive terms smaller. Halving uses the multiplier \(\frac12\).
lessons.method:
What operation gives the same multiplier?

Compare at least two ratios. Equal differences suggest a linear rule. Equal non-zero ratios in a nonconstant sequence suggest repeated multiplication.

Why does the exponent start at zero?

Substitute \(n=1\) to check that the factor is \(r^0=1\). Substitute \(n=2\) to check that the multiplier is used once.

How do I find where a power occurs?

The exponent gives the number of steps from position 1. Add one to reach the position number. For the small integer powers here, a list of powers is enough.

Can the repeated multiplier make the terms smaller?

In \(a(\frac12)^{n-1}\), substitute the position before evaluating the power. Multiplying by one half is the same as dividing by two.
mistakes: When the differences are getting bigger, check the ratios before choosing a model.
Using \(ar^n\) with \(a\) as the first term applies one multiplication too early.
The exponent and the position number differ by one when the rule starts at n = 1.
Dividing by a half doubles the term. To halve a value, multiply by a half or divide by two.

examples.title: Fill the gap in a constant-ratio sequence
examples.question: The terms \(10,\;50,\;\square,\;1250,\;6250\) are consecutive in an exponential sequence. Find the missing term.
examples.solution:
The first two values give the multiplier \(5\). Apply it once to \(50\).

The missing value is \(250\). Multiplying this by \(5\) gives the fourth term.

examples.title: Find the rule for a constant multiplier
examples.question:
The sequence \(23,\;46,\;92,\;184\) has a constant multiplier. Which expression gives its \(n\)-th term?

  1. \(23\times 2^{n-1}\)
  2. \(23\times 2^n\)
  3. \(23+2(n-1)\)
  4. \(2\times 23^{n-1}\)
examples.solution:
Divide the second value by the first. The multiplier is \(2\), and the first term is \(23\).

There are \(n-1\) multiplications from the first term to term \(n\). The rule is \(23\times 2^{n-1}\).

examples.title: Find a position in an exponential sequence
examples.question: A sequence has \(T_n=17\times 3^{n-1}\). At which position does the term \(1377\) occur?
examples.solution:
Divide \(1377\) by the first term \(17\). The factor is \(81\), which equals \(3^4\).

The exponent is 4, so \(n-1=4\) and the position is \(5\).

examples.title: Find a term when the multiplier is below one
examples.question: The sequence starts \(288,\;144,\;72,\;36\) and always uses the same multiplier. Find the exact term value at position 9.
examples.solution:
Each term is half of the term before it. The nth-term rule is \(288\left(\frac12\right)^{n-1}\).

At position 9, halve the first term 8 times. The value is \(\frac{9}{8}\).

lessons.title: Connect and combine sequences
lessons.summary: Extended: combine terms at a common index, track index changes and find the rule for numerators and denominators.
lessons.objective: Extended: combine terms at a common index, track index changes and find the rule for numerators and denominators.
lessons.before: For Extended. Check that you can find and use a linear rule and recognise square and cube numbers.
lessons.ideas:
If \(C_n=A_n-2B_n\), use the same position \(n\) in both component sequences. Then take twice the B term away from the A term.

The rule \(B_n=A_{n+2}\) uses a later term of A. Position 1 of B takes position 3 of A.

Read all the given numerators as one sequence and all the denominators as another. Use the fractions as displayed so that you can see both patterns.
lessons.method:
Which values do I combine?

Work out the two values first when asked for one position. For a polynomial expression, substitute the two formulas and collect like terms.

What does a change of subscript do?

Work out the new position before using the first sequence's formula. Write both positions explicitly so you can keep track of them.

How do I find a rule for a sequence of fractions?

Find a rule for each row at the same position, then put the numerator rule over the denominator rule. Use brackets around any whole expression you type into an answer field.
mistakes: A multiplier in front of B changes its whole value. It does not change the index or only one term of its formula.
Adding two to an index and adding two to a term value are different operations.
Reducing each given fraction first can hide the pattern in its original numerator and denominator.

examples.title: Combine a linear and an exponential term
examples.question: Let \(A_n=19\times 4^{n-1}\) and \(B_n=5n+11\). If \(C_n=A_n-2B_n\), find \(C_{6}\).
examples.solution:
At position 6, the values are \(A_{6}=19456\) and \(B_{6}=41\).

Subtract twice the value of B from the value of A. This gives \(19374\).

examples.title: Track a change of index between two sequences
examples.question: A sequence has \(A_n=5n^2+6\). A second sequence has \(B_n=A_{n+1}\). Find \(B_{5}\).
examples.solution:
In B, use the position 5 first. This points to position 6 in A.

Evaluate A at that position to get \(186\).

examples.title: Find a rule for a sequence of fractions
examples.question: The first four terms are \(\frac{16}{11},\;\frac{20}{14},\;\frac{24}{19},\;\frac{28}{26}\). The numerators form a linear sequence. The denominators are shifted square numbers. Find the \(n\)-th term as a single fraction.
examples.solution:
The numerators \(16,\;20,\;24,\;28\) have rule \(4n+12\).

The denominators \(11,\;14,\;19,\;26\) have rule \(n^2+10\). Put the two rules together to get \(\frac{4n+12}{n^2+10}\).

    [2]

Subtract one term from the term that follows it. Each change is \(9\).

The last step shown adds 6. The next step subtracts 5.

(a)

Find the change by subtracting the earlier term from the later term.

(b)

Look at the action between the last two terms, then swap to the other action.

questions.title: Count panels and compare strips
questions.prompt_html:
1. A row of signs has 8 end lights altogether. At stage \(n\) it also has 5 lights in each of \(n\) repeated panels. The first three totals are \(13,\;18,\;23\). How many lights are there at stage 13?

    [2]

  2. Two strips grow in stages. Strip A has \(27,\;34,\;41\) tiles at stages 1 to 3 and grows by 7 tiles each stage. At the same stage, strip B has twice as many tiles as A, plus 7. Find the number of tiles in strip B at stage 4.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:

The panels give \(5n\) lights at stage \(n\). The end lights do not change.

Use \(5n+8\). For stage 13, the total is \(73\).

(b)

1. Let \(A_n=17\times 5^{n-1}\) and \(B_n=3n+5\). If \(C_n=A_n-2B_n\), find \(C_{7}\).

    [2]

  2. A sequence has \(A_n=2n^2+17\). A second sequence has \(B_n=A_{n+3}\). Find \(B_{19}\).

    [2]

  3. The first four terms are \(\frac{23}{5},\;\frac{30}{8},\;\frac{37}{13},\;\frac{44}{20}\). The numerators form a linear sequence. The denominators are shifted square numbers. Find the \(n\)-th term as a single fraction.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

At position 7, the values are \(A_{7}=265625\) and \(B_{7}=26\).

Subtract twice the value of B from the value of A. This gives \(265573\).

(b)

In B, use the position 19 first. This points to position 22 in A.

Evaluate A at that position to get \(985\).

(c)

The numerators \(23,\;30,\;37,\;44\) have rule \(7n+16\).

The denominators \(5,\;8,\;13,\;20\) have rule \(n^2+4\). Put the two rules together to get \(\frac{7n+16}{n^2+4}\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Work out the two term values at the stated position before combining them.

(b)

The shift acts on the position before the formula is used.

(c)

Read the top and bottom of each term as separate sequences. Use the given fractions as written.

Add the index offset to the requested position and evaluate the original rule there.
Find the rule for the complete numerators and for the complete denominators, then put them over one fraction bar.

marking_criteria.guidance_html: Accept any equivalent expression with the same position numbering.
